record.paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
record.original_question: Do measurable solar-flare properties provide predictive insight into the later effects of those eruptions on the near-Earth environment, and can that knowledge be turned into operational guidance that better protects technological assets and infrastructure from space-weather impacts?

evidence.quote: • Do ﬂare properties provide insight into their subsequent impacts on near Earth environment, and thereby help us to protect assets and infrastructure [81, 82]?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of solar flare events, each characterized by a vector of measurable properties at or near the Sun, including but not limited to: peak soft X-ray flux and GOES class, flare duration and impulsive-phase timescales, spatial location on the solar disk (heliographic longitude/latitude), associated active-region magnetic complexity (e.g., Hale/Mount Wilson class, magnetic free energy, photospheric current helicity), presence and properties of an associated coronal mass ejection (speed, mass, angular width, direction, magnetic field orientation), and accompanying solar energetic particle signatures. For each such event, define a vector of near-Earth space-weather impact metrics observed within a fixed forecast window after the flare onset, such as the disturbance storm-time index Dst, the planetary K-index Kp, ionospheric total electron content perturbations, geomagnetically induced current amplitudes, and >10 MeV proton fluxes at geosynchronous orbit.

(a) Determine whether there exists a statistically significant predictive mapping from the vector of solar flare properties (optionally augmented by associated CME and SEP observables) to the vector of near-Earth impact metrics, and quantify the achievable forecast skill (e.g., Brier score, true skill statistic, ROC area) as a function of lead time and of which solar observables are included.

(b) Identify a minimal subset of flare-related observables sufficient to attain a prescribed level of forecast skill, and characterize the irreducible predictive uncertainty given current observational capabilities.

(c) Translate any such predictive mapping into an operational decision rule that prescribes protective actions for technological assets and infrastructure (e.g., satellites, power grids, aviation, communications) so as to minimize an expected loss functional balancing impact mitigation against the cost of false alarms.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad open research question in heliophysics and space-weather forecasting. While many empirical and machine-learning models relate flare properties (and associated CME/SEP signatures) to geomagnetic indices, no comprehensive predictive mapping with operational reliability has been established; recent reviews and forecasting community roadmaps still list it as an outstanding challenge.

status_evidence.title: Space Weather Operations and Research Infrastructure (NASEM)
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies prediction of geoeffective consequences of solar eruptions from solar observations as an unsolved operational challenge.
status_evidence.claim: Translating flare/CME observables into reliable near-Earth impact forecasts remains an open operational problem.

status_evidence.title: Camporeale (2019), The Challenge of Machine Learning in Space Weather
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews the state of ML-based space weather forecasting and notes substantial gaps in linking solar observables to geomagnetic impact with operational skill.
status_evidence.claim: Predictive skill from flare properties to near-Earth impacts is partial and an active research area.
